schools.summary: Gill fixes 'an appointed time' on the fixed bounds of a life, a set term whose limits cannot be passed, and hears in 'Enosh' the frail, mortal creature.
Henry hears 'a warfare, so the word is' — man on the earth God gave him, his time appointed by God not blind fortune, life a soldier's and day-labourer's service.
Clarke lays bare 'tsaba' as warfare and reads life a state of probation, exercise to train us for eternity; Wesley keeps a time limited by God in this miserable world.
Keil and Delitzsch settle that 'tsaba' is not field-labour but active military service, then toil in general — life as a hard campaign whose discharge is death.

debates.question: Does the word (tsaba) denote a fixed appointed span of life, or a warfare / term of hard service (life as probation)?

sides.position: an appointed, limited time — the fixed bounds of a life
a warfare / hard military service — life as probation and exercise

schools.summary: Gill hears in the desired 'shadow' either the midday shade from the scorching sun or the evening/sunset shadow ending the day's toil — so death is no more sinful to wish than the hireling's evening.
Clarke takes the 'shadow' for night itself (Virgil, Servius: night is the shadow of the earth), the evening when wages are paid and rest comes; Wesley: the shadow is the sunset, the time for rest.
Henry: as a tired servant longs for the evening when he receives his penny and goes to rest, so Job may long for death — 'the sleep of the labouring man is sweet.'
Keil and Delitzsch bind the simile to its point — Job waits for death as rest after hard labour — yet note he stops on this side of that consoling conclusion.

sides.position: the evening / sunset shadow, ending the day's toil and bringing wages and rest
either the midday shade for relief or the evening shadow

themes: death as the evening of toil

schools.summary: Gill marks that the 'so' does not answer the similes — Job's lot is the reverse, months of emptiness not shadow, tossing not rest — and the measure of months tells how the days dragged.
Henry locates the 'vanity' in uselessness: days a burden because he can do no good; Job grieves less that they lack pleasure than that they do no good, and so are months of vanity.
Keil and Delitzsch take the word in its force of nothingness / disappointment — 'months of disappointment' that one after another cheat the sick man's hope of recovery.
Clarke keeps to experience: the night no relief but a continuance of labour, Job like the hireling with his task and the soldier harassed by the enemy, ever on the watch.

sides.position: months of emptiness / uselessness — days that do no good
'months of disappointment' — the hope of the sick man cheated month by month

schools.summary: Gill catches the cry — as soon as Job lies down he says 'Oh that it were time to rise!' — the bed that should ease him only wearying him and lengthening the night.

Henry: sleep gives some intermission to our sorrows, 'the parenthesis of our sorrows,' but Job gains no such relief, tossing to and fro till morning like a fretful spirit ever shifting and never easy.
Clarke: a man under continual affliction with no respite, finding ease in no posture, 'full of tossings' — nothing better depicts unremitting suffering.
Ellicott renders the couplet 'the night is long, and I am filled with tossings to and fro till the morning twilight.'
Gill reads it of Job's present misery — ulcers breeding worms, scabs crusted like a garment, the running matter clotting with dust and ashes into clods — a saint in a vile body.
Henry draws the lesson: see what vile bodies we have, carrying the seeds of their own corruption, that we may not pamper or be proud of them.

Clarke breaks with the commentators, reading 'clods of dust' as the dried scales and crusts of the elephantiasis; Wesley keeps the plain sense — worms bred of the corrupted flesh, the dust of the earth, the skin broken by ulcers.
Ellicott: it is characteristic of elephantiasis that the skin grows hard and rugous, then cracks and ulcerates; Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering as the record of a real disease.

debates.question: What are the 'clods of dust' clothing Job's flesh?

sides.position: literal earth / dust and ashes caked upon the running sores
the hard scales and crusts of the disease itself (elephantiasis)

themes: a saint in a vile body

schools.summary: Gill takes the swift days not of his slow-creeping affliction but of his common days, especially his days of prosperity, soon over and sometimes wished back.

Clarke argues 'areg' names the weaver rather than the shuttle, doubts the shuttle existed, and gathers the web-and-thread figure (the three Fates, Isa. 38:12, Coverdale); Wesley keeps the shuttle passing in a moment, 'without hope' of any good day.
Henry turns the shuttle into meditation: every day leaves a thread behind, and we weave either the spider's web that fails or the robes of righteousness — every man shall wear as he wove.

debates.question: Does the word (areg) name the 'weaver' or the 'shuttle'?

sides.position: the shuttle, thrown swiftly across the web
the weaver rather than the shuttle

themes: the thread of life cut off

schools.summary: Gill reads it as an address to God: life is breath in the nostrils, a vapour and bubble; God cannot forget, but may seem to when his hand is heavy, and to remember when he lifts it — which Job here begs.
Henry: a dying man commends himself to God's compassion as a fleeting creature, his life 'a wind that passeth away and cometh not again' (Ps. 78:39); we must shortly see good no more.
Clarke reports Good's rendering — 'if my life pass away, mine eye shall turn no more to scenes of goodness' — but judges the common 'my life is wind' a very good sense.
Keil and Delitzsch fix it: 'Remember that my life is a breath, that my eye will never again look on prosperity' — we see good only in this life, which ends with death.

debates.question: How should the verse be rendered?

sides.position: the common reading — 'O remember that my life is wind'
Good's turn — 'if my life pass away, mine eye shall turn no more to scenes of goodness'

themes: we see good only in this life

schools.summary: Gill takes the quick eye that shall see Job no more after death, with the caution that the dead are still seen of God, of angels, and of glorified saints; the sense is seen no more among the living.
Henry unfolds the removal to an unseen state (Ps. 39:13), and hears 'thine eyes are upon me, and I am not' as God able to look him into eternity and frown him into the grave.

Clarke offers 'Thou canst look me into nothing' or 'let thine eye be upon me as one judged to death,' and adds the pathos that Job may die with his friends' odium unanswered; Wesley: 'thou canst look me into eternity.'
Ellicott renders 'thine own eyes shall look for me, but I shall be no more' (LXX, Vulg.); Keil and Delitzsch the same — eyes that seek and find the place empty, not a look that annihilates.

debates.question: What does 'thine eyes are upon me, and I am not' mean?

sides.position: a look that annihilates — God can look him into nothing / into eternity
eyes that seek and look for him, only to find him gone

themes: seen no more among the living

schools.summary: Gill: a cloud once dispersed is never seen again, new clouds succeeding it; the point is less the suddenness than the irrevocableness of life once gone.
Ellicott prizes the simile — nothing more completely passes away than the summer cloud, whether it vanishes in the sky or falls in rain; an appearance that comes to nought.
Clarke: as the cloud shall never return, so the dead return no more to sojourn among the living; Wesley guards 'no more' as 'never until the general resurrection' and preaches the vanishing cloud.
Henry: dying is done but once and had need be well done; the same cloud never returns, a new generation raised as the former passes away — secure a better place when we die.

themes: a vapour that appears and vanishes

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'house' in several senses — the dwelling a good man will not wish back, the body raised only at the resurrection, or the family in which he bears no more part.

Ellicott: the words (echoed in Ps. 103:16) must not be forced to forbid a future life; they are accurately true of man here, and it is of this world that Job speaks — his Maker has looked on his misery.

Clarke: not that Job shall be annihilated, but never again an inhabitant of the earth; the word for 'grave' may mean the state of the dead or any pit. Wesley: he shall be known no more here — secure a better place, for this will own us no more.
Henry rounds it out: others take the house till they too resign it; glorified saints return no more to its sorrows, nor sinners to its pleasures — it concerns us to secure a better place.

themes: return no more to his house
his place knows him no more
the words not denying a future life

schools.summary: Gill sets out the reasoning and records Jarchi's 'just retaliation' — since God will not refrain his hand, Job will not refrain his mouth — yet judges it Job's infirmity, where he should have been dumb like David.

Henry weighs it against David's silence (Ps. 39:9): with few breaths to draw we should spend them in gracious breathings of faith, not the noxious breathings of corruption — better die praising than quarrelling.
Clarke: all is hopeless, so Job indulges his complaint; Wesley: since life is short and past recovery, he will plead for pity before he dies and ease himself by pouring out his complaint.

debates.question: Is Job's refusal to keep silence pardonable or blameworthy?

sides.position: a pardonable easing of an overburdened heart
the infirmity of a good man who should have been still under God's hand

themes: I will not refrain my mouth

schools.summary: Gill runs through the images — restless sea, raging sea, leviathan, emblem of cruel tyrants — and answers that Job was the reverse, gentle in prosperity, yet hedged and watched as if dangerous.

Clarke reports the Targum's Egyptians/Pharaoh but prefers the common version — Job hedged in like a beast in a net, his afflictions the bars set on the sea (Jer. 5:22; Job 38:11); Wesley: am I as unruly as the sea, to be restrained by heavy miseries?

Ellicott explains it from Egypt — the Nile called 'the sea,' watched by dykes lest it overflow; Keil and Delitzsch: a watch on the sea can only be to hold its swelling within bounds, the indignity Job feels.

Henry draws the lesson: we are apt in affliction to complain that God restrains us more than there is need, whereas we are never in heaviness but when there is need, nor more than the necessity demands.

debates.question: What lies behind 'a sea, or a whale... that thou settest a watch over me'?

sides.position: the Egyptians / Pharaoh drowned in the Red Sea
the bounded sea or the guarded Nile, kept within its decreed limits

themes: am I a sea or a whale

schools.summary: Gill reads the sick man's reasonable hope — that he would lie down and get a little sleep to comfort and refresh him, as he had known in better days — a hope that failed.
Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole movement: the bed that should comfort and the couch that should ease his complaint, then the dreams that overthrow the hope, setting up the cruel reversal.

Henry dwells on the disappointed expectation — sleep is appointed to relieve us and often has — but Job's bed terrified and his couch added to his complaint; God can meet us with terror even where we look for ease.
Gill traces the dreams to the distemper and pain, to melancholy, or to Satan permitted to disturb him — all ascribed to God because he suffered it — so the dreams added to his sufferings.
Clarke: Satan was permitted to haunt his imagination with terrific appearances, so that he feared to close his eyes — could a state more deplorable be conceived?
Keil and Delitzsch render 'thou scaredst me with dreams, and didst wake me up in terror from visions' — the night-visions startling him out of what little sleep he had.

Henry holds both hands together — the distemper opened the door, Satan delighting to terrify whom he cannot destroy, and Job referring all to God who permitted it; hence pray our dreams neither defile nor disquiet us.
Gill is careful this is no self-murder — not to strangle himself like Ahithophel, but to welcome death in any shape, even a suffocating disease, so weary is he of life.
Clarke gives it a physical cause — an oppression and difficulty of breathing like the incubus or nightmare — which he would prefer to longer life in such misery.

Ellicott marks the Hebrew literally 'than my bones,' or 'a death by these my members' (suicide); Keil and Delitzsch render 'death rather than this skeleton,' the wasted frame Job would exchange for the grave.
Henry names it Job's infirmity — a good man would choose death rather than sin, yet should be content to live as long as God pleases, since life is our opportunity of glorifying God.

debates.question: What does Job weigh against death in the last clause?

sides.position: 'rather than my life' — death welcomed in any form
literally 'than my bones' — the wasted frame / skeleton

themes: the choice of despair an infirmity

schools.summary: Gill offers several senses of 'I loathe it' — Job loathes his life, or his bones, or 'I am become loathsome' to all around him, or 'I pine and waste away.'
Clarke reads the loathing of life itself, which Job would spurn even with length of days if joined to such suffering; and notes Good's 'No longer would I live! O, release me!'
Ellicott finds a ray of comfort in 'I shall not live for ever' against the AV's wish; Keil and Delitzsch render 'I would not live alway; let me alone, for my days are breath.'
Henry: a good man would not, if he might, live always in a world of sin and temptation, having a better world in prospect — yet Job's judgment was here overborne by passion.

debates.question: Is the second clause a wish or a comfort?

sides.position: a wish that recoils from life — 'I would not live always'
a comforting statement of fact — 'I shall not live for ever'

themes: a ray of comfort in mortality

schools.summary: Gill reads the marvel as grace — that God should magnify frail, fallen, sinful man, set his heart on any of the race, and through his Son's incarnation espouse them to himself and share his glory.
Henry lays out both readings — a passionate reflection that God demeans himself contending with mean man, or a pious admiration of grace that God takes man into covenant and visits him as a friend.

Clarke sets the two senses side by side (man not worth thy notice / how astonishing thy kindness, with Calmet's paraphrase); Wesley leans to complaint — man not worthy of God's favour, yet below his anger.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the key: the questions parody Psalm 8 (and the mercies new every morning, Lam. 3:23) — where David marvels God so exalts man, Job complains God makes too much of him.

debates.question: Is 'What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?' a complaint or a pious admiration?

sides.position: an ironic / passionate complaint — God demeans himself over, or makes too much of, a creature not worth it
a pious admiration of divine condescension and grace

themes: what is man that thou magnifiest him

schools.summary: Gill lets both senses stand — visiting in love (the Redeemer, effectual calling, mercies new every morning) and visiting in chastisement (the rod every morning) — both true of God's close dealing with man.

Henry takes the visiting, in Job's mouth, as the relentless return of affliction like a daily ague, yet hears beneath it the truer note that God's visiting man at all is a condescension no creature could claim.
Keil and Delitzsch read the questions as the dark underside of Psalm 8 — the ceaseless visiting and trying not honour but a burden, God's perpetual attention that will not let his creature be.
Wesley gathers the strands: God visits with mercy to preserve his spirit and tries him by afflictions and by prosperity alike, observing his motions every moment as in care and jealous over him.

debates.question: Is the 'visiting every morning / trying every moment' gracious visitation or afflictive scrutiny?

sides.position: gracious visitation — mercies new every morning
afflictive scrutiny — the daily rod and relentless testing

schools.summary: Gill hears a cry to be released from God's wrestling hand, rendering with Broughton 'how long wilt thou not look off from me?' — the angry look of grappling wrestlers, from which Job begs relief.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'how long dost thou not look away from me'; Ellicott takes 'till I swallow down my spittle' as a proverb like 'the twinkling of an eye' or 'while I fetch a breath.'

Clarke fixes the Arab proverb — the least imaginable space, a moment to moisten the parched tongue and speak again; Wesley: how long ere thou withdraw thy afflicting hand, that I may have a breathing time?
Henry feels the image of a man who cannot swallow — Job's distemper in his throat almost choked him (ch. 30:18) — pleading, 'wilt thou not give me some respite?' (ch. 9:18).

themes: how long wilt thou not depart

schools.summary: Gill takes 'I have sinned' as a real acknowledgment, though not of notorious crimes — Job owns daily sin as the best men do, no match for a holy God, unable to answer one fault of a thousand.

Ellicott renders 'putting the case that I have sinned, yet what can I do unto Thee, O keeper of men?' (glancing at v.12); Keil and Delitzsch call 'I have sinned' hypothetical, an inferential question, not an admission of guilt.

Clarke reports Kennicott (words to Eliphaz, 'thou spy upon mankind') and gives 'Be it that I have sinned, what injury can I do, O Observer of man?'; Wesley finds a genuine confession within the supposition — free of crying sins, yet obnoxious to justice.

Henry hears the title as Preserver — God's eye upon man for good — so the complaint carries a seed of hope; and bids us enquire 'what shall I do?' eyeing God as Saviour, not destroyer: 'be my Saviour.'

debates.question: Is 'I have sinned' a real confession or a hypothetical concession?

sides.position: a genuine acknowledgment of daily sin
a hypothetical 'granted that I have sinned,' not admitting the charged guilt

debates.question: Is the divine title 'Preserver / Saviour of men' or 'Observer / Watcher of men'?

sides.position: Preserver / Saviour of men — the eye upon man for good
Observer / Watcher / 'spy upon' men — scrutiny from which nothing hides

outliers.note: Reports Kennicott's view that the words are addressed to Eliphaz, not God — 'I have not sinned against thee, O thou spy upon mankind' — so that Job does not here criminate himself.

themes: what shall I do unto thee

schools.summary: Gill dwells on 'pardon' as literally 'lift up' — the burden of guilt lifted off, laid on the Son who bore it and took it away, removed as far as the east is from the west; for this lifting Job sues.

Henry: Job means more than the removal of trouble, being earnest for the return of God's favour (ch. 6:4); where God removes the guilt he breaks the power of sin, and Job urges the plea by the nearness of the dust.

Clarke reads it 'after the manner of men' and insists Job does not criminate himself — Bildad answers him as justifying, not confessing; Wesley: 'seeing thou art gracious to others, why may not I hope the same?'

Ellicott: in Job's belief sin was the origin of all disaster, so pardon would end his sorrows — a belief our Lord did not discourage (Mark 2:5); Keil and Delitzsch render 'thou shalt seek me, but I shall not be,' the speech suspended between penitence and despair.

debates.question: Does the closing plea amount to a confession of guilt?

sides.position: a genuine plea for pardon of a real transgression
a plea urged 'after the manner of men' by one still maintaining his innocence

themes: thou shalt seek me but I shall not be
